title: A doctor’s guide to surviving — and enjoying — holiday feasting while on GLP‑1 medication | CNN
authors: Reed Berger-Fleishman, University of Illinois Chicago
text:
EDITOR’S NOTE:The views expressed in this commentary are solely those of the writer. CNN is showcasing the work ofThe Conversation, a collaboration between journalists and academics to provide news analysis and commentary. The content is produced solely by The Conversation.

Thanksgiving and the winter holidays bring celebration, connection and plenty of opportunities to come together with family and friends.

But the holiday season also brings something else: more food-centered gatherings, larger portions and richer foods than most people typically eat throughout the year. Think whipped sweet potatoes, mac and cheese, decadent side dishes and an abundance of desserts.

For people taking GLP-1 medications for diabetes management, weight loss or other medical reasons, these celebrations can present unique challenges. Changes in appetite, smaller portion tolerance, limits on alcohol consumption, medication side effects and thedesire to maintain progresscan make navigating holiday traditions feel a little different.

As aphysician specializing in obesity medicine, I encourage my patients to view GLP-1 medications as an advantage during the holidays. These medications can help regulate appetite, improve awareness of fullness, and reinforce healthier eating behaviors during a season when food often takes center stage.

However, these medications don’t eliminate the possibility of overindulgence. In fact, patients who previously experienced little or no nausea due to GLP-1s may suddenly develop significant nausea or even vomiting after eating beyond their new comfort level. Nothing canderail a holiday celebrationquite like an upset stomach. Accounting for how these medications affect your body can help you avoid uncomfortable surprises while still enjoying the foods and traditions you love.

Whether taken by injection or orally, GLP-1 medications have become increasingly popular worldwide for managingType 2 diabetes, obesity and other chronic conditions. In the United States,approximately 1 in 10 adults used these drugsin 2025, and prescribing rates continue to climb.

GLP-1 medications work by reducing hunger, slowing stomach emptying and helping patientsfeel full sooner and stay full longer. Many patients also reportfewer cravings for high-calorie foodsand even areduced desire to drink alcohol.

In many ways, these effects can make holiday food temptations easier to navigate. My patients often tell me that they already know which dietary changes they need to make, but GLP-1 medications help them put those changes into practice. They find it easier to stop eating when they’re satisfied, resist unnecessary snacking and avoid the constant thoughts about food that previously made weight management so challenging.

One of the most important things you can do during the holidays is to learn to recognize your body’s changingfullness signals. Pay attention to nausea, bloating and early fullness rather than pushing yourself to finish everything on your plate.

Read more:Why don’t GLP‑1 obesity drugs work for everyone?

These symptoms can serve as reminders that you’ve reached your comfortable limit. The best plan is to enjoy smaller portions, eat slowly and pause between bites to give your body time to recognize fullness. Rich, high-fat foods in particular can worsen nausea and prolong the sensation of fullness. A few bites of your favorite dishes may be much more satisfying than an entire serving.

GLP-1 medications don’t make these decisions for you – but they can reinforce healthier behaviors.

Alcohol deserves special consideration during the holidays, when social gatherings andcelebrations often revolve around drinking. Although you may have tolerated alcohol without difficulty in the past, GLP-1 medications can change your experience.

Some patients report that GLP-1 medicationsreduce their desire for alcoholaltogether. For them, the holidays may represent their first opportunity to drink since starting treatment.

The safest approach is to be cautious and recognize that alcohol can aggravate medication-related gastrointestinal symptoms.

Holiday travel can disrupt established routines, medication schedules and access to prescriptions. A little planning can help prevent unnecessary interruptions in treatment.

When in doubt, plan ahead and ask for guidance rather than making medication adjustments on your own.

Perhaps the most important advice I give my patients is this: The holidays are not everyday life, and one large meal or dessert will not erase the progress you’ve made.

Read more:Don’t stress out about overeating during the holidays

You don’t need to skip Thanksgiving dinner, avoid your favorite dessert or feel guilty about enjoying a special meal. Maintaining a healthy relationship with food means allowing yourself flexibility while keeping your long-term goals in perspective.

At the same time, don’t let one celebratory meal turn into several weeks of abandoning the habits that have helped you succeed. Enjoy the occasion, recognize when you’ve had enough, and return to your usual routine afterward.
